title: The woman who carried an ox
hookLine: custom makes anything seem natural, until you travel (Essays 1.23)
carry: what feels like nature is often custom

cards: Shoes off at the door, or shoes on in the house. Dinner at six, or dinner at ten. The fork in the left hand, or switched to the right.

A kiss on one cheek, or two, or a handshake. To someone, each of these is simply how things are done. Then a trip, or a new in-law, or a roommate from somewhere else, and the obvious thing turns out to be a choice.
Montaigne wrote an essay about that moment, and he opens it with a woman carrying a calf.

teach.b: First, the story. A village woman, Montaigne tells us, got used to petting and carrying a calf from the day it was born, and because she never stopped, she was still carrying it when it was a full-grown ox.
Whoever first told that story, he says, understood the power of custom. It grows a little every day, until we're carrying something enormous without noticing the weight. Second, the schoolmistress.
Custom, Montaigne writes, is a violent and sly teacher. She sets up her authority softly, bit by bit, then shows a tyrant's face, and we no longer dare raise our eyes to her. Third, the handkerchief.

He tells of a gentleman who blew his nose with his fingers and defended it: why wrap something dirty in fine linen and carry it around in our pockets? Montaigne admits the argument has some sense to it.
Only habit had kept him from seeing how strange the handkerchief is.

We notice strangeness in other countries' customs, he says, and miss it in our own. He goes further: even the rules of conscience, which we say come from nature, are born of custom. Fourth, the brake.
Montaigne doesn't tell anyone to tear up the town's laws.
A wise person, he says, keeps their judgment free inside, and outwardly still follows the accepted ways. Questioning a custom and overthrowing it are different things.
Day to day, just custom is the pause before calling someone else's way weird.

how: Readers of Montaigne take his essay on custom as an invitation to see one's own habits as habits, while noting that he also counsels caution about overturning accepted laws.

practice: Look around the room, or around your day, for one thing you do without ever deciding to: the way you fold towels, which side of the bed, what counts as on time. Ask Montaigne's question gently: is this nature, or just custom?
You don't have to change it; just see it as a choice for a moment.

wordCard.voice: Just custom. Montaigne's essay on habit: it grows like a calf into an ox, until what we were taught feels like nature, and we only see it when we meet another way. Today's word.

orig.note: French: a schoolmistress, Montaigne's picture of custom in this essay.

carryVoice: Your line: what feels like nature is often custom. Your own way was taught too, one day at a time. Until tomorrow.
